# Shell Primer {#sec-shell .unnumbered}

Every chapter in this book runs commands at a shell prompt:
`docker build`, `git commit`, `Rscript`, `quarto render`. The
book assumes a reader can already type these and read what
comes back, but a 2026 syllabi comparison found that only 7 of
30 comparable reproducibility courses actually teach the shell;
the rest, like this book until now, assume it. This appendix is
the missing prerequisite: enough of the Unix shell to follow
every command shown elsewhere in the book, in the order those
commands are needed, with nothing beyond that scope [the
treatment below follows the scope and sequencing of
@swcarpentry2024shell, a widely used open lesson covering the
same ground].

## Where you are: `pwd`, `ls`, `cd`

A shell session has a current working directory, the folder
commands act on by default. `pwd` ('print working directory')
reports it as an absolute path, one that starts from the
filesystem root and names every folder down to the current one:

```bash
pwd
#> /Users/jane/project
```

`ls` lists the contents of the working directory, or of a path
given as an argument:

```bash
ls
#> analysis  R  DESCRIPTION  renv.lock
ls analysis
#> data  report
```

Plain `ls` hides entries whose name starts with a dot, such as
`.gitignore` or the `.here` marker Chapter 5 relies on. `ls -a`
('all') shows them, along with the two special entries every
directory has, `.` for itself and `..` for its parent:

```bash
ls -a
#> .  ..  .gitignore  .here  analysis  R  DESCRIPTION  renv.lock
```

`cd` ('change directory') moves the working directory. `cd
analysis/report` moves into a subfolder named relative to where
you already are; `cd /Users/jane/project` moves to an absolute
path regardless of where you started; `cd ..` moves up one
level, to the parent of the current directory; and `cd` with no
argument returns to the home directory. `cd ../..` chains two
steps up, and `cd ../report` moves up one level and back down
into a sibling folder, without ever returning to the project
root by name.

The distinction between a relative path (`analysis/report`,
`../data`) and an absolute path (`/Users/jane/project`) matters
throughout this book. A relative path resolves differently
depending on the working directory the shell happens to be in
when the command runs, which is exactly the fragility Chapter 5
examines in its section on project-oriented paths: a script
that is correct when launched from the project root can be
wrong when launched from `analysis/report/`, because a relative
path has no fixed meaning on its own. `here::here()` fixes this
inside R by computing an absolute path from a marker file, but
the underlying hazard, that a relative path depends on where you
started, is a shell concept first and an R concept second.

## File operations: `cp`, `mv`, `rm`

`cp source destination` copies a file, leaving the original in
place. `mv source destination` moves or renames a file; the
file at `source` no longer exists afterward, only the one at
`destination` does. Both accept a directory as the destination
to copy or move a file into it, keeping its name:

```bash
cp cohort_raw.csv backup/cohort_raw.csv
mv draft.qmd final.qmd
```

A single asterisk, `*`, is a wildcard the shell expands to
every matching file name before the command ever runs it:

```bash
ls *.csv
#> cohort_raw.csv  cohort_clean.csv
```

`rm *.csv` therefore does not pass the literal text `*.csv` to
`rm`; the shell expands it first, into the list of matching
file names, and `rm` deletes each one named in that list. The
distinction matters because the expansion happens silently
before the command runs, so `*.csv` in the wrong directory
deletes a different, unintended set of files, not nothing.

`rm file` deletes a file. This is the one command in this
section that deserves a direct warning: unlike `git`, the shell
has no undo. A commit can be reverted, a branch can be
recovered from the reflog, but a file removed with `rm` is
simply gone; it does not pass through a trash folder, and no
earlier chapter's recovery techniques apply to it. Running `rm
*.csv` in the wrong directory, or `rm -rf` on the wrong path,
destroys exactly what it is told to destroy, correctly and
irreversibly. Treat `rm` as one-way, and prefer moving a file to
an explicitly named `trash/` folder over deleting it outright
when the cost of being wrong is high.

## Redirection and pipes: `>`, `>>`, `|`

Every command in a shell produces output on a stream called
standard output, which prints to the terminal by default.
Redirection sends that stream somewhere else instead. `>`
writes standard output to a file, replacing the file's entire
contents if it already exists:

```bash
echo 'first line' > out.txt
cat out.txt
#> first line
echo 'second line' > out.txt
cat out.txt
#> second line
```

The second `>` above did not add a line; it overwrote the file,
and `first line` is gone. `>>` appends instead of overwriting,
adding its output after whatever is already in the file:

```bash
echo 'third line' >> out.txt
cat out.txt
#> second line
#> third line
```

This single character, `>` versus `>>`, is the difference
between replacing a log file and growing one, and it is worth
checking deliberately rather than guessing, because the failure
mode of using `>` by mistake is silent: the file exists, it
has content, and nothing in the command's own output signals
that the previous content was discarded.

A pipe, `|`, sends one command's standard output directly into
the next command's standard input, without an intermediate
file:

```bash
printf 'apple\nbanana\ncherry\n' | grep an | wc -l
#> 1
```

Here `printf` produces three lines, `grep an` keeps only the
lines containing `an` (just `banana`), and `wc -l` counts the
lines that survive, reporting 1. Chains like this appear
throughout the book's CI configuration and `Makefile` targets,
where a build step's output is filtered or counted without ever
being written to disk.

A command has a second stream, standard error, for diagnostics
and failures, kept separate from standard output so that
redirecting one does not silently swallow the other. `2>`
redirects standard error alone:

```bash
cat does_not_exist.txt 2> err.txt
cat err.txt
#> cat: does_not_exist.txt: No such file or directory
```

Without the `2>`, that same error message prints to the
terminal as usual; a plain `>` on its own redirects only
standard output and leaves error messages visible, which is why
a redirected command can still fail loudly even though its
output file is empty.

## Environment variables and `PATH`

An environment variable is a named value the shell makes
available to every program it runs, not just to the shell
itself. `export NAME=value` sets one and marks it for export,
meaning child processes, programs the shell launches, inherit
it too:

```bash
export MYVAR=hello
echo "$MYVAR"
#> hello
bash -c 'echo "in subshell: $MYVAR"'
#> in subshell: hello
```

Without `export`, a variable assignment (`MYVAR=hello`, no
`export`) is visible only to the current shell, not to programs
it starts. This is the mechanism behind an instruction this book
gives more than once without naming it: setting
`RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED=FALSE` before an R session, as
Chapter 12's continuous-integration examples do, works because
the shell exports it into the environment that `R` or `Rscript`
then reads when it starts. The variable is not an R setting; it
is a value the shell handed to the R process at launch, and any
process the shell starts can read it with its own language's
equivalent of `echo $VAR` (`Sys.getenv('RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED')`
in R).

`PATH` is a particular environment variable, a colon-separated
list of directories the shell searches, in order, when it looks
up a command name. Typing `Rscript` works because some directory
in `PATH` contains a program named `Rscript`; `echo $PATH` shows
the search list, and prepending a directory to it (`export
PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"`) makes programs placed there runnable by
name without typing their full path.

## Permissions and the execute bit

`ls -l` shows a permissions string before each file name, such
as `-rw-r--r--`. The first character marks the entry type (`-`
for a plain file, `d` for a directory); the next nine are three
groups of three, read, write, and execute permission for the
file's owner, its group, and everyone else.

A script with no execute permission cannot be run directly, even
if the file itself is readable text:

```bash
ls -l greet.sh
#> -rw-r--r--  1 jane  staff  37 Oct 12 07:48 greet.sh
./greet.sh
#> permission denied: ./greet.sh
```

`chmod +x greet.sh` adds execute permission for the owner, the
group, and others, after which the same command runs:

```bash
chmod +x greet.sh
ls -l greet.sh
#> -rwxr-xr-x  1 jane  staff  37 Oct 12 07:48 greet.sh
./greet.sh
#> hello from script
```

The `x` bit is what separates 'this file contains runnable
instructions' from 'this file is runnable right now'; a shell
script downloaded or generated by a template typically starts
without it, and `chmod +x` is the usual fix.

`chmod` also accepts a three-digit numeric mode, one digit per
group (owner, group, other), each digit the sum of read (4),
write (2), and execute (1) for that group. `chmod 644 greet.sh`
sets `-rw-r--r--`, read and write for the owner and read-only
for everyone else, with no execute bit anywhere; `chmod 755
greet.sh` sets `-rwxr-xr-x`, the common mode for a script meant
to be run by its owner and read and executed, but not modified,
by anyone else. The symbolic form (`+x`, `-w`) changes one bit
at a time without needing to know the rest; the numeric form
sets all nine bits in one command.

## A note on bash versus zsh

The commands above work the same way in bash and in zsh, the
two shells most readers will encounter, and this book's own
examples assume bash-compatible syntax throughout. This matters
on macOS specifically: Apple switched the default shell from
bash to zsh in macOS Catalina (2019), so a reader following this
book on a current Mac is, by default, typing these commands into
zsh, not bash. The everyday commands in this appendix, `pwd`,
`ls`, `cd`, `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, redirection, pipes, `export`,
`chmod`, behave identically in both. Differences surface only in
more advanced scripting, array syntax and certain glob options
differ, which this book does not otherwise rely on. A reader who
hits a syntax error on a book command that looks exactly as
written should suspect a shell difference before suspecting a
typo, and can check which shell is running with `echo $SHELL`.
